    Ransomware Attacks Move Beyond Enterprise Systems to Theaten Employees' Families

    📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (510 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Attackers are exploiting enterprises' own artificial intelligence systems and extending pressure beyond internal networks to employees and their families, according to a new Semperis survey of organizations that suffered disruptive ransomware attacks.
    • In a recent announcement, the manufacturer highlighted findings from its 2026 Ransomware Risk Report, which examines AI-related attack tactics, personal intimidation, and recovery preparedness.
    • It has been revealed that the sample has an crucial limit: This year's study included only organizations where at least one ransomware attack caused business disruption.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Attackers are exploiting enterprises' own artificial intelligence systems and extending pressure beyond internal networks to employees and their families, according to a new Semperis survey of organizations that suffered disruptive ransomware attacks.

    In a recent announcement, the manufacturer highlighted findings from its 2026 Ransomware Risk Report, which examines AI-related attack tactics, personal intimidation, and recovery preparedness. Censuswide surveyed 1,200 information technology and security professionals across nine countries and eight industry sectors in the first half of 2026.

    It has been revealed that the sample has an crucial limit: This year's study included only organizations where at least one ransomware attack caused business disruption. The results describe those victims' experiences, rather than the likelihood that an organization will suffer an attack. The report says that sampling approach changed from previous studies.

    Semperis sells identity security, recovery and crisis management products.

    The report says 84% of respondents experienced attacks that exploited AI in some way. Its breakdown distinguishes AI-based attacks, reported by 40%, from attacks that manipulated victims' own AI agents or systems, reported by 44%. That distinction matters: The broader figure covers both attackers using AI and attackers exploiting AI deployed inside an organization.

    Industry observers note that defensive use of AI also produced mixed responses. Nearly half of respondents, 49%, noted they successfully used AI for detection or response, while 23% said their AI tools failed to detect or respond successfully. Those are survey responses about victimized organizations, rather than a controlled comparison of security products.

    Recent findings suggest that chris Inglis, former U.S. national cyber director and a Semperis strategic adviser, described the difficulty of recognizing AI's involvement. "Many attacks are not perceived as being aided and abetted by AI because they're just too slick, too sophisticated," he remarked in the report.

    Data erasure, destruction, or release remained the most frequently reported threat, at 56%. Blackmail, extortion or public shaming followed at 41%, with system lockouts or operational sabotage at 40%. The report also recorded psychological intimidation at 23% and physical threats at 17%.

    In a recent development, in an Aug. 20 Dear Colleague Letter from Kirsten Baesler, assistant secretary of the United States Department of Education's Office of Elementary and Secondary Education, ED outlines upcoming guidance to frame the national conversation around the educational value of technology in schools.

    It has been revealed that as generative AI has become embedded in the tools students use to search, write, create, translate, organize, and receive feedback, the boundary between "using AI" and "not using AI" has become increasingly difficult to define. More importantly, treating AI use as a binary choice does little to help students understand the different roles AI can appropriately play in learning.

    Artificial intelligence is raising the stakes of cyber conflict as attackers use the technology to accelerate reconnaissance, uncover vulnerabilities, and launch attacks faster than many security teams can respond, according to a latest report from agentic AI security manufacturer Kai.

    E-mail phishing threats reached 7.3 billion in Q3 2026, with September activity increasing 41% from August, according to Microsoft Threat Intelligence.

But it has been American owned since 1983 and has a distinct quality tied deeply to its long history in the U.S. market—which puts it slightly outside the predictable purview of many watch collectors.

    Right now, a growing band of horological nerds is finding rich pickings in the Movado back catalog and pushing up vintage prices considerably—especially for its mid-century chronographs and its legendary Museum Watch (which celebrates 80 years in 2027; more of that to come) in the process.

    According to recent reports, it’s not only the collectors who are digging into Movado’s past, however. Last month, the brand released the Heritage Tempo-Matic ($995–$1,095), a re-creation of a watch that merges sporty and retro design in a neat and slinky package. The Tempo-Matic, Movado’s first automatic movement, was rolled out in 1945 and went on to power a broad range of Movado’s wristwatches. But the rounded yet boxy “TV” shape of the upcoming Heritage Tempo-Matic is unmistakably 1970s, when watch design took a giant leap forward into sexy new territory.

    The 2026 version is available in three executions, each powered by the reliable Sellita SW200-1B movement and fitted with integrated steel bracelets that positively scream seventies. Two of them come in brushed steel with vertically brushed burgundy or blue dials. A third—which, we must admit, is our favorite—is gold-tone PVD with a warm gray dial. You’d be hard-pressed to find such an elegant, authentic, and affordable homage to the 1970s—a decade that’s right now a very hot motif in watch-collecting circles—anywhere else.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Nearly 70% of organizations report a significant gap between artificial intelligence spending and measurable financial returns, according to a recent survey by IDC.
    • The research firm's 2026 Worldwide AI Economics and Cost of Ownership Survey found that 69% reported such a gap, while only 15% had achieved an AI return on investment exceeding 100%.
    • In a separate May 2026 survey, 73% of respondents identified excessive AI costs as a significant risk.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Nearly 70% of organizations report a significant gap between artificial intelligence spending and measurable financial returns, according to a recent survey by IDC.

    The research firm's 2026 Worldwide AI Economics and Cost of Ownership Survey found that 69% reported such a gap, while only 15% had achieved an AI return on investment exceeding 100%.

    In a separate May 2026 survey, 73% of respondents identified excessive AI costs as a significant risk.

    IDC highlighted the findings in an October 20 analysis examining what enterprise customers expect from AI technology vendors.

    Enterprise customers are placing greater emphasis on measurable business outcomes when evaluating AI products, according to IDC.

    The firm identified three priorities for vendors: demonstrating financial value, addressing governance and security requirements, and building support beyond IT departments.

    The analysis also highlighted the gap between initial agentic AI deployments and broader adoption. Although 80% of organizations have started deploying agentic AI, only 17% are using it across the enterprise.

    IDC remarked evaluating AI investments can be difficult when the technology changes how employees work and how business processes operate.

    The firm expects AI infrastructure capacity to catch up with demand around 2029, potentially easing costs. Until then, vendors face pressure to demonstrate the long-term financial value of their products.

    Sources indicate that AI funding decisions involve a broad range of executives. IDC's September 2026 C-Suite Tech Survey found that CIOs and CTOs were involved in 63% of those decisions, business-function executives in 62%, and chief financial officers in 61%.

    A separate IDC survey found that 42% of CEOs planned to hire a chief AI officer within the next 12 months.

    Buyers also reported concerns about the products and terms vendors offer. Limited integration with existing systems, insufficient model and data transparency, and concerns about vendor lock-in were each cited by 34% of respondents.

    Overpromising and underdelivering, along with unclear pricing models, were each cited by 31%.

    IDC said vendors need to substantiate financial returns and address security and governance requirements while working with decision-makers across IT, finance, and other business departments.

    For more information, go to the IDC blog.

    Industry observers note that in an Aug. 20 Dear Colleague Letter from Kirsten Baesler, assistant secretary of the United States Department of Education's Office of Elementary and Secondary Education, ED outlines new guidance to frame the national conversation around the educational value of technology in schools.

    It has been revealed that as generative AI has become embedded in the tools students use to search, write, create, translate, organize, and receive feedback, the boundary between "using AI" and "not using AI" has become increasingly difficult to define. More importantly, treating AI use as a binary choice does little to help students understand the different roles AI can appropriately play in learning.

    Artificial intelligence is raising the stakes of cyber conflict as attackers use the technology to accelerate reconnaissance, uncover vulnerabilities, and launch attacks faster than many security teams can respond, according to a newly introduced report from agentic AI security firm Kai.

    E-mail phishing threats reached 7.3 billion in Q3 2026, with September activity increasing 41% from August, according to Microsoft Threat Intelligence.

    Report: Global Ransomware Attacks Rise 23% in Q3

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Global ransomware activity increased 23% in the third quarter of 2026, with organizations in North America and Europe accounting for the largest share of attacks, according to cybersecurity firm NCC Group.
    • The tech giant's Cyber Threat Intelligence Report Review of Q3 2026 recorded 2,865 ransomware victim claims, up from 2,325 in the previous quarter.
    • Despite the quarterly increase, attacks declined 26% month over month in September to 821.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Global ransomware activity increased 23% in the third quarter of 2026, with organizations in North America and Europe accounting for the largest share of attacks, according to cybersecurity firm NCC Group.

    The tech giant's Cyber Threat Intelligence Report Review of Q3 2026 recorded 2,865 ransomware victim claims, up from 2,325 in the previous quarter.

    Despite the quarterly increase, attacks declined 26% month over month in September to 821. North America recorded the most attacks that month with 390, followed by Europe with 211.

    In a recent development, the industrial sector accounted for 29% of quarterly attacks, while Qilin remained the most active ransomware group for the sixth consecutive quarter, recording 365 victims. The Gentlemen followed with 356, and INC Ransom ranked third with 109.

    The report highlighted a July cyber attack against a small UK power generation facility that forced operations to stop for approximately four days.

    Although the incident did not affect the national electricity grid, it demonstrated how cyber attacks can disrupt physical infrastructure.

    The security researchers said the incident was consistent with techniques previously associated with Iranian-affiliated campaigns, including attacks against internet-exposed industrial controllers.

    However, the UK government has not formally attributed the attack, and the techniques used remain unconfirmed.

    The report also identified growing security challenges as organizations connect traditional IT networks with operational technology (OT) systems for remote maintenance and centralized management.

    The firm recommended network segmentation, stronger privileged-access controls, and continuous monitoring of OT environments.

    The research found that more than 40 vulnerabilities affecting enterprise applications, VPN appliances, e-mail gateways, and management platforms were added to CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog during the quarter.

    The report examined Gunra, a ransomware-as-a-service operation that has targeted 53 victims across multiple industries as of Q3.

    According to the cybersecurity organization, Gunra exploited vulnerabilities CVE-2024-55591 and CVE-2025-24472 in internet-facing Fortinet devices to gain access to corporate networks.

    The group also used stolen credentials, session hijacking, and administrative tools to move between systems before deploying ransomware.

    Other emerging ransomware groups included Deadlock and Storm, with the latter claiming 78 victims by the end of September.

    Researchers also observed initial access brokers advertising compromised VPN, Remote Desktop Protocol, and SSH access, alongside access to cloud identities, source code repositories, and security management platforms.

    The quarterly review also highlighted BraZetsu, an AI-enhanced Windows malware framework that evolved into a specialized initial access toolkit.

    According to the report, BraZetsu uses AI models to automate victim profiling, analyze compromised environments, and identify valuable corporate systems.

    The framework searches for enterprise software, financial data, digital certificates, and cloud credentials, helping operators identify compromised access that can be sold to other cyber criminals.

    The cybersecurity firm also identified risks involving legitimate AI agents, including prompt injection, excessive permissions, and unintended access to external systems.

    The report cited incidents involving U.S. and Australian government systems as examples of agents accessing resources beyond their intended scope.

    Researchers warned that these incidents do not necessarily involve malicious intent but can create consequences resembling conventional cyber intrusions.

    For the full report, visit the NCC Group site.

    Network-provider trust concerns are impacting enterprise AI looks, with AI and data-driven projects the most affected initiatives among respondents reporting disruption, according to a report from telecommunications provider Arelion.

    According to recent reports, her song choice for the post, “I Can’t Make You Love Me” by Bonnie Raitt, was pointed and aspirationally petty, too. Some of the lyrics? Ahem: “Cause I can’t make you love me if you don’t / You can’t make your heart feel something it won’t.”.

    Another pro, Britt Stewart, added, “It’s the scream for me.”.

    ICYMI, one of The Sun’s sources previously alleged Jenna had been “gunning for a Broadway role, 100 percent” when she performed a mini solo at the end of her and Harry’s performance of “Supercalifragilisticexpialidocious” earlier in the season.

    It has been revealed that “She has become more and more focused on her getting a Broadway offer after this season and after the DWTS tour ends than she is highlighting Harry and it shows,” a source told the outlet. “She put a solo of herself into the routine for Disney Night—which is basically unheard of for a pro to do.     Tech Report: Microsoft Expands Protections and Controls for Sovereign Cloud

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Microsoft is introducing latest tools within its sovereign cloud offerings designed to give organizations tighter control over where their data resides, who can access it, and how critical systems operate, especially in light of AI becoming a bigger part of enterprise infrastructure.
    • Industry observers note that in a recent announcement, Douglas Phillips, president and chief technology officer of Microsoft Specialized Clouds, outlined updates spanning public cloud, private cloud, and partner environments.
    • "Digital sovereignty should give organizations greater control and security over the technology they depend on, while continuing to innovate," Phillips wrote.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Microsoft is introducing latest tools within its sovereign cloud offerings designed to give organizations tighter control over where their data resides, who can access it, and how critical systems operate, especially in light of AI becoming a bigger part of enterprise infrastructure.

    Industry observers note that in a recent announcement, Douglas Phillips, president and chief technology officer of Microsoft Specialized Clouds, outlined updates spanning public cloud, private cloud, and partner environments. The changes target governments, regulated industries, and organizations that need tighter control over sensitive workloads without abandoning cloud-based AI capabilities.

    "Digital sovereignty should give organizations greater control and security over the technology they depend on, while continuing to innovate," Phillips wrote.

    It has been revealed that one of the biggest additions is Microsoft's Sovereign Control Panel, which will enter public preview at Microsoft Ignite. Available through the Azure portal, the tool will give IT administrators one place to manage data sovereignty settings, spot compliance challenges, and identify potential risks that could disrupt operations.

    According to recent reports, microsoft is also tightening controls over who can access sensitive systems. Its Data Guardian feature will require oversight by personnel based in Europe when Microsoft engineers access certain production systems in the European Union and European Free Trade Association. Another tool, Production Touch Ledger, will keep tamper-resistant records of that access, giving organizations a clearer picture of who accessed their systems and what they did.

    Industry observers note that microsoft is also giving customers more control over encryption. External key management with Azure Managed HSM is now generally available, letting organizations keep their main encryption keys on hardware they own or manage outside Microsoft's cloud.

    Sources indicate that the manufacturer is also expanding its Sovereign Private Cloud offerings, giving organizations more options to run systems with or without an internet connection. Fresh capabilities include GitHub Enterprise Local, GitHub Copilot with locally hosted AI models, and additional data services running on Azure Local.

    The push for greater operational control comes as Microsoft is also reconsidering how enterprises should secure increasingly autonomous AI systems.

    As reported by Redmond magazine, Microsoft is expanding Project Perception to address risks posed by what the company calls "agentic insiders," AI agents capable of accessing sensitive information and performing actions without constant human supervision.

    That initiative introduces aims for Guardian Agents, specialized security agents designed to monitor other AI systems, evaluate their behavior and intervene when their actions become risky.

    "Monitoring and securing those agents must become continuous," mentioned Hayete Gallot, executive vice president of Microsoft Security.

    Project Perception is about limiting what AI agents can do. Microsoft's sovereign cloud expansion tackles a different set of questions: where those systems run, who gets to administer them, and how the data stays protected.

    Industry observers note that taken together, the two efforts point to a shift in Microsoft's enterprise AI strategy. The firm is putting more weight on oversight, not just automation.

    Phillips mentioned AI is making these questions more pressing as organizations roll out intelligent systems across sensitive business processes and critical infrastructure.

    For more information, go to the Microsoft blog.

    Chris Paoli (@ChrisPaoli5) is the associate editor for Converge360.

    Industry observers note that technology directors touch nearly everything that happens in a school system. Here are three strategies these IT leaders can use to navigate their many duties without losing strategic focus, influence, or sustainability.

    E-mail phishing threats reached 7.3 billion in Q3 2026, with September activity increasing 41% from August, according to Microsoft Threat Intelligence.

    Cloud Security Alliance's 2026 Top Threats report ranks identity as the leading cloud security concern, followed by two new AI-related risks.

    Network-provider trust concerns are impacting enterprise AI plans, with AI and data-driven projects the most affected initiatives among respondents reporting disruption, according to a report from telecommunications provider Arelion.

    It has been revealed that of all of the brands we frequently shop, Lululemon might just be one of the most sale averse—so when the retailer unveils an honest-to-goodness Black Friday sale, it’s worth paying attention. Sure, you can often score pieces from Lululemon’s “We Made Too Much” section, but that’s mostly limited to “get it before it’s gone” colors and styles.

    Starting November 19, through Cyber Monday on November 30, Lululemon is offering up to half off editor-approved styles, whether you’re shopping for holiday gifts, want to replace your worn-out joggers, or are already looking ahead to your “Work out more” Fresh Year’s resolution and need to update your gym wardrobe accordingly.

    Shop Lululemon’s Black Friday sale.

    At some point, Lululemon morphed from solely being the retailer we’d turn to for workout wear to a place where you could feasibly handle most of your wardrobe needs, courtesy of the brand’s fan-favorite ABC pants, comfortable button-downs, and solid range of outerwear, all of which are included in the brand’s Black Friday markdowns.

    We’ve gone so far as to dub these pants “iconic,” thanks to their versatility. They’re almost like denim in that way—easy to wear with casual pieces but also able to be dressed up in a pinch. Per Jonathan Evans, style director, the ABCs are a “smart, performance-minded essential that you can comfortably pull on every day.” Need we say more?

    Of course, Lululemon’s true bread and butter will always be athleisure. Right now, editor-endorsed joggers, T-shirts, and shorts—for those who are partial to showing a little leg year-round—are available for a fraction of the price.

    According to recent reports, if you’re looking for sweats that can withstand snow and sleet, opt for the License to Train Joggers, our pick for the brand’s most durable joggers. They’re made from abrasion-resistant, water-repellent fabric—an essential for anyone who trains outdoors. And if you’re in need of a new coat, everything from puffers to windbreakers and vests starts at $99.

We’re willing to bet there are multiple folks in your life who have Lululemon at the top of their wish list (especially the Gen Z crowd; you’re welcome).     Freestyle: “Like a Prayer” and “Music” by Madonna.

    Judges’ Choice: Quickstep to “Sing Sing Sing” by Louis Prima.
